svg.title: Four management architectures in order of resilience, and the access chain that sits on top of whichever one you choose
svg.desc: Four rungs, worst to best. Rung one: management in-band on a production VLAN, reachable from the user subnet - simplest to build, and it fails exactly when production fails, which is the moment you need it. Rung two: in-band with a management ACL - the blast radius shrinks to a named set of sources, but the path still shares fate with the traffic it manages. Rung three: a management VRF or a dedicated management VLAN with its own routing - the fate is separated at layer 3, though it often rides the same physical links and the same power. Rung four: fully out-of-band through a separate console or terminal server network - independent of production routing, independent of production power where possible, and the only rung that still works when the thing you are managing has failed. Right: the access chain that applies to every rung - a bastion host, two factors, per-command authorization, session recording, and a rate-limited ACL on the management interface. Bottom: the two questions that decide the rung - what is the budget, and what is the recovery objective for a device that is unreachable. A footer notes that rung one is chosen in about 80 percent of the networks that later describe a management outage as a surprise.
svg.text: Management access fails at the worst possible moment, unless it was designed not to
Every rung is defensible. What is not defensible is not knowing which rung you are on.
RUNG 1 Management in-band, reachable from the user subnet
cheapest to build, and it fails exactly when production fails - the moment you need it
any host on the LAN can reach the device's own door
RUNG 2 In-band with a management ACL
blast radius shrinks to a named set of sources; the path still shares fate with the traffic it manages
loses to a routing failure, an overloaded link, or a full CPU
RUNG 3 Management VRF or dedicated management VLAN
fate separated at layer 3, with its own routing table and often its own addressing
still rides the same physical links and the same power feed
RUNG 4 Fully out-of-band: console server on a separate network
independent of production routing and, ideally, of production power
the only rung that still works when the device itself has failed
THE ACCESS CHAIN (on any rung)
1 bastion host - no direct engineer to device sessions
2 two factors, with the second not being SMS
3 per-command authorization from TACACS+
4 session recording for privileged access
5 rate-limited mgmt ACL, logging drops
6 break-glass in a sealed envelope, alarmed on use
The chain is identical on all four rungs: the rung
decides resilience, the chain decides who gets in.
Mixing them up is how a hardened rung 1 stays one
password away from total loss.
TWO QUESTIONS THAT PICK THE RUNG
What is the budget, including
the console server and its cabling?
it is smaller than one outage
What is the recovery objective for
a device nobody can reach?
a truck roll is four hours, at best
A middle path worth naming: out-of-band for the core
and edge only, management VRF for access. It covers
the devices whose loss actually stops the business.
The test that settles an argument in a review: unplug the production uplink from the core, then try to log in. Whatever you can still reach is your real management architecture.
Second test: take away the engineer's own laptop and the jump host, and see whether a documented path remains. If not, the design has one credential and one device as its foundation.
